<reason>A won the comparative justification clash. B compellingly rejected a permanent local veto and highlighted A’s Yellowstone concession, but A supplied an approval standard rather than requiring unanimity. More importantly, A showed that targeted browsing control could begin restoration without waiting for reintroduction, while predator coexistence also requires continuing funding and cooperation. B’s safeguards strengthened its position, but its repeated contrast between self-repair and indefinite ecological delay did not adequately answer those alternatives.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s response to B’s whole-policy comparison was decisive: maintaining fences, guarding livestock, and paying compensation remain ongoing institutional obligations, while targeted management can allow seedlings to recover now. This undercut both B’s claimed funding asymmetry and its argument that delaying imposed reintroduction necessarily sacrifices forest regeneration.</best_rebuttal>
